summary:
Hosea prophesied in the northern kingdom of Israel in its final decades. The opening verse (1:1) places him under Judah's kings Uzziah through Hezekiah and Israel's Jeroboam II, roughly the 750s BC onward. After Jeroboam's death four kings were assassinated (2 Kings 15); in 722 BC Assyria destroyed the capital, Samaria, and deported the people (2 Kings 17). Hosea usually calls the kingdom "Ephraim," after its leading tribe. His message begins with a command about his own life: "Go, take a prostitute as your wife and have children of adultery, because this land is flagrantly prostituting itself by departing from the LORD" (1:2).

In chapters 1–3 Hosea marries Gomer, and their three children carry messages as names. Jezreel ("God sows") announces punishment on Jehu's dynasty for "the bloodshed of Jezreel" (1:4), Jehu's massacre at that valley (2 Kings 9–10). Lo-ruhamah ("No Compassion") and Lo-ammi ("Not My People") follow: "for you are not My people, and I am not your God" (1:9). Hosea 2:23 overturns both names — "I will say to those called 'Not My People,' 'You are My people'" — and Paul quotes the reversal in Romans 9:25–26. In chapter 3 Hosea is told to love an adulterous woman again "as the LORD loves the Israelites, though they turn to other gods" (3:1), and buys her back "for fifteen shekels of silver and a homer and a lethech of barley" (3:2). Two details are debated: how Gomer was unfaithful (prostitute before the marriage, unfaithful wife after it, or one of the "shrine prostitutes" of 4:14), and whether the unnamed woman of chapter 3 — in Hebrew simply "a woman" — is Gomer or someone else.

Chapters 4–14 are poetic speeches that open like a lawsuit: "the LORD has a case against the people of the land" (4:1). The charges mix idolatry and politics: worship of Baal, the Canaanite storm god; the calf idol of Samaria (8:5–6), descended from Jeroboam I's golden calves (1 Kings 12:28–29); priests who "feed on the sins of My people" (4:8); and diplomacy that flits between empires, "a silly, senseless dove — calling out to Egypt, then turning to Assyria" (7:11). What God asks for is hesed — Hebrew for loyal, committed love — rendered "loving devotion" in 4:1 and "mercy" in 6:6: "For I desire mercy, not sacrifice, and the knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings." Jesus quotes that verse twice (Matthew 9:13; 12:7).

Chapter 11 trades marriage imagery for parenthood: "When Israel was a child, I loved him, and out of Egypt I called My son" (11:1), which Matthew applies to the child Jesus' return from Egypt (Matthew 2:15). God recalls teaching Ephraim to walk (11:3) and asks, "How could I give you up, O Ephraim?" Israel will not be wiped out like Admah and Zeboiim, cities overthrown with Sodom (Deuteronomy 29:23): "My heart is turned within Me; My compassion is stirred!" (11:8). Chapter 13 still ends with Samaria falling by the sword. Yet 13:14 asks, "Where, O Death, are your plagues? Where, O Sheol, is your sting?" — Sheol is the Hebrew realm of the dead. Whether that promises rescue or summons Death to strike is disputed; Paul quotes it as a taunt over a beaten enemy (1 Corinthians 15:55).

The book ends with an invitation. "Return, O Israel, to the LORD your God" (14:1), with the prayer supplied: "Take away all our iniquity" (14:2). God replies, "I will heal their apostasy; I will freely love them" (14:4) — apostasy means desertion, turning away. The last verse speaks to the reader: "Whoever is wise, let him understand these things," for "the ways of the LORD are right, and the righteous walk in them but the rebellious stumble in them" (14:9).
